outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS. What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov, then apply for an EIN at irs.gov the same week. The entity name and EIN are needed for every permit, license, bank account, and lease signature that follows. If you are a sole proprietor, you may skip the entity formation and file a fictitious business name (DBA) statement with the San Francisco County Clerk instead, but an LLC or corporation is standard for a bar with a liquor license and limits personal liability.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN). What to say: Apply online at businessportal.sfgov.org within 30 days of starting business in San Francisco. The fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, $625 at $1–1.5M for 2026–27, each plus a $4 state fee). Every other city department asks for your BAN, so do this immediately after forming the entity and getting the EIN. The registration year runs April 1 to March 31 and renewal is due by the last day of February each year.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain the health permit to operate from the San Francisco Department of Public Health. What to say: Apply online at sfdph.org/dph/EH at least one month before opening, with your BAN, Location ID (LIN), and federal tax ID. The permit is issued after plan check (if the space is new or remodeled) and a final inspection. For a bar with no food preparation, the 2026–27 fee is $470 for the Permit to Operate application (includes initial inspection) and $0 annual license fee for 2026–28. A certified food safety manager is not required if you serve only beverages, but if you serve any food (even prepackaged snacks), at least one owner or employee must have a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent, $100–$250) before the pre-opening inspection. Schedule the final health inspection two weeks in advance; DPH will refer the permit application to Planning for zoning review, and Planning will confirm the CUA approval.
outcomes.note: The cited record is about business registration certificate, not health permits; it does not describe the health permit process, fees, or requirements.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain music licensing (ASCAP and BMI) and complete RBS training for all alcohol servers and managers. What to say: Federal copyright law requires a blanket public performance license to play music (background, DJs, live covers, TV with music). Apply online at ascap.com and bmi.com; annual fees are formula-based on occupancy and music use (typically $300–$2,500 per catalog). Most venues need both ASCAP and BMI because their catalogs do not overlap. California AB 1221 requires Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) certification for every alcohol server and their managers within 60 days of hire. Register on the ABC RBS Portal at abc.ca.gov/licensing/rbs ($3), complete an approved course (about $10–$25), and pass the exam. Keep the certification list on site for ABC inspections. These are fast (1–7 days each) but easy to forget, so schedule them in the final two weeks before opening.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,163 to $15,700. Notes: The timeline and cost range cover the Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000), the Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit (45–120 days, $2,708), and the health permit to operate (14–45 days, $470), which are the approvals in the entitlement path. These are times to approval for cases that are granted; denied or withdrawn cases are not included in this range. The CUA is the critical path: pre-application meeting, environmental review, community meeting, 300-foot mailed notice, 30-day posted notice, and Planning Commission hearing, followed by a 30-day appeal period, typically take six to ten months when approved. The Entertainment Commission permit follows the CUA and adds two to four months (intake meeting, referrals to five departments, 30-day posted notice, and Commission hearing). The health permit is administrative and takes two to six weeks after the CUA is approved. The cost does not include the ABC license because the description does not state whether the existing Type 48 license will be transferred, amended, or remain unchanged, so no ABC cost is included. If a Type 48 transfer is needed, add 90–180 days and $17,000–$450,000 (license purchase price plus transfer fees). The cost also does not include business registration ($55–$700), entity formation ($70–$150), a fictitious business name ($60–$120), workers' compensation insurance (premiums are a percentage of payroll, not a government fee), music licensing ($600–$5,000 for ASCAP and BMI combined), or RBS training ($13–$150 for five employees), because these are not discretionary approvals and are required for any bar. The timeline assumes no discretionary review, no neighborhood appeal to the Board of Supervisors, and no revisions required by the Entertainment Commission; protests or appeals can add three to six months.
